content.title: Response to Reviewer iAA1
content.comment:
1. **Clarification on LogitClip vs LogitNorm.**

Thank you for bringing this recent paper [1] into the discussion and we also note that Reviewer 8C9K has recognized LogitClip is novel compared to logit normalization. We would like to further clarify that our work is fundamentally different from the LogitNorm paper, where they employ logit normalization to improve the OOD detection performance. Technically, the logit vectors of all training inputs are normalized to be a unit vector with a constant norm. Our work bears three major differences, in terms of the problem setting, methodology, and theoretical insights. 

* **Problem setting**: LogitNorm focuses on improving the performance of detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) examples during the test time, while our work aims to enhance the robustness against noisy labels in the training stage. In other words, the **learning tasks are fundamentally different**. 

* **Methodology**: We propose to clamp the logit vector to ensure it is upper bounded by a constant, while LogitNorm normalizes the logits of all examples. Choosing the way of clipping-by-norm is the only reason why our approach seems technically similar to the LogitNorm. As discussed in Section 5, we also consider the variant of clipping-by-value and provide a detailed comparison between the two different clipping operations in LogitClip. Referring to the relationship between Gradient Clipping [2, 3] and Gradient Normalization (NGD) [4, 5], our LogitClip is a unique method that is different from LogitNorm.

* **Theoretical insight**: LogitNorm aims to decouple the influence of logits’ magnitude from network optimization, and they empirically show that their method leads to more meaningful information to differentiate in-distribution and OOD samples. In contrast, our LogitClip is designed to enforce an upper bound of the resulting loss, as shown in Proposition 3.1. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical interpretation to further understand why LogitClip introduces the noise-tolerant ability and which kinds of loss functions LogitClip can work with. In summary, our analysis builds a connection between LogitClip and noise robustness, which is novel as appreciated by Reviewers mAac and 8C9K.

With the three major differences, we can conclude that our work is novel and provides a sufficient contribution to the problem of learning with noisy labels. **As suggested by the reviewer, we have cited the LogitNorm paper [1] in the revised version and add the above discussion in Appendix H**. 


2. **Most theoretical analyses are straightforward to derive.**


We strongly believe that our theoretical analyses are important and contributive, directly and coherently supporting our proposed method. Specifically, our analyses not only theoretically explain why LogitClip brings the noise-tolerant ability, but also show which kinds of loss functions LogitClip can work with. In this way, our theoretical analyses build a clear connection between the logit clipping and the provable robustness against noisy labels. Without the formal analyses, our in-depth understanding of the proposed method would be ambiguous.

(continue with the next post)

content.title: Response to Reviewer iAA1
content.comment:
3. **How is the proposed method compared to other alternatives?**

Thank you for raising an interesting point here. As appreciated by Reviewer 8C9K, we have compared the proposed method to: 1) RELU6, 2) Clipping-by-value (Figure 3 of Section 5), 3) Logit norm regularization (Figure 4 of Appendix G.2). The results consistently demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method and we also provide a discussion about the reason. 

* ReLU6: although ReLU6 provides a constraint on the outputs of the intermediate layers, the resulting loss is unbounded yet since the final output can be multiplied through the last linear layer (Weight decay is not enough to bound the parameter values, which is similar to the norm regularization).
* Clipping-by-value (LC-V):  LC-V is suboptimal as the clipping operation may diminish the gradients on the clipped components of the logit vector. Besides, LC-V would also modify the direction of the input vector and even change the final prediction. 
* Norm Regularization (NormReg): NormReg encourages the model to give prediction with a small logit norm for all training examples, which may cause a similar effect to weight decay. Different from the LogitClip method, NormReg cannot induce an upper bound on the loss value so it does not introduce the noise-tolerant ability.

As suggested by the reviewer, we also conducted an additional experiment to check the method that normalizes the feature vectors and the results are shown in the table below. We find FeatureNorm cannot be comparable to our method across the four settings. Theoretically, weight decay does not provably induce a bound on the weight so that the final output is unbounded yet. 

To the best of our knowledge, LogitClip is the first method to bound the loss at the logit level, in the context of learning with noisy labels. We expect our method can inspire more specially designed methods to explore robust loss from the logit perspective. For example, our method has inspired the reviewer to consider FeatureNorm for robust losses, which might be a good start.

| Method | Sym-50% | Asymmetric | Dependent | Real |
| -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| FeatureNorm     | 81.66     | 84.55     | 79.26     | 78.09     |
| LogitClip     |  84.37     | 86.91     | 86.74     | 82.06     |


[1] Wei, Hongxin, et al. "Mitigating Neural Network Overconfidence with Logit Normalization.", ICML 2022.

[2] Abadi, Martin, et al. "Deep learning with differential privacy." CCS 2016.

[3] Zhang, Jingzhao, et al. "Why gradient clipping accelerates training: A theoretical justification for adaptivity." ICLR 2020.

[4] Hazan, Elad, et al. "Beyond convexity: Stochastic quasi-convex optimization." NeurIPS 2015.

[5] Murray, Ryan, Brian Swenson, and Soummya Kar. "Revisiting normalized gradient descent: Fast evasion of saddle points." IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control (2019).

- As to the clarification, I'm still not convinced that the authors *did not* know the work of LogitNorm [1] when developing this LogitClip, since there are many overlapping notations between these two papers, and other works of Wei et al. like [2][3] were cited in the submitted version. LogitNorm, and the authors DID NOT know LogitNorm before working on LogitClip*; otherwise, I would consider this paper as a dishonest plagiarism.

- As to the listed novelty (Problem setting, Methodology, Theoretical insight), the provided arguments are not strong enough. The methods of LogitNorm and LogitClip are quite similar, and most of the theoretical insights in this paper are straightforward. However, I would not consider novelty as a critical point for accepting or rejecting this paper, since this is a subjective assessment.

- I thank the authors for providing new results on comparing FeatureNorm and LogitClip, which is good. But I disagree the claim that `weight decay is not enough to bound the parameter values'. Imposing weight decay in the loss function is equivalent to optimizing the Laplacian with hard constrains on the parameter norms. Therefore, empirical comparisons with other alternatives are still necessary.

Refences:

[1] Wei, Hongxin, et al. Mitigating Neural Network Overconfidence with Logit Normalization.

[2] Wei, Hongxin, et al. Combating noisy labels by agreement: A joint training method with co-regularization.

[3] Wei, Hongxin, et al. Metainfonet: Learning task-guided information for sample reweighting.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 8C9K
content.comment:
1. **More detailed explanation for why CE causes the noise overfitting.**

Thank you for pointing out the writing suggestion. As suggested by the reviewer, we will rewrite the motivation part in the final version due to page limit. Specifically, the gradients of CE can be shown as: $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(f(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta}), y)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}}=-\frac{1}{\sigma_{y}(z)} \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \sigma_{y}(z)$. From the equation, we show that examples with smaller prediction confidences are weighted more than examples with larger prediction confidence for the gradient update. In other words, CE pays more attention to hard examples (or noisy examples). This can be an advantage of CE when training with clean data. However, it converts to a robustness issue when we move to the label noise setting. In the extreme case of $\sigma(z) \to 0$, the unbounded loss (and weight) would be infinite, which means that the loss optimization focuses on those examples with noisy labels. In this way, training with CE loss leads to serious overfitting on noisy labels.


2. **Explain why a small $\tau$ may result in difficulties for loss optimization.**

Thank you for pointing out the ambiguous statement. The difficulties of loss optimization are caused by the large lower bound (from a small $\tau$). For example, on the CIFAR10 dataset, the lower bound of the loss value would be about 2.30 if we set $\tau=0.0001$. With such a large loss value, the model will underfit the training data. Another extreme case is $\tau \to 0$, where the upper bound would be equal to the lower bound. As a result, the optimization cannot update the loss values of all training examples, so the model learns nothing. This is why a small $\tau$ would result in difficulties in loss optimization. We will make this clearer.

3. **A guideline for the choice of $\tau$.**

Our analysis in Proposition 3.1 can provide a guideline for tuning the $\tau$. As shown in the proposition, the lower bound of the loss value is dependent on the hyperparameter $\tau$ and the class num K. Consequently, we can calculate a rough range of the hyperparameter $\tau$ to achieve a small lower bound. For example, on the CIFAR-10 dataset, the $\tau$ should be larger than 0.83 if we require the training loss to be smaller than 1.0. With such an estimation, we can then adjust the value of $\tau$ to find a "sweet spot".



4. **What happens when we increase the depth of the same architecture (e.g.,ResNe18-->ResNet34 --> ResNet50)?**

We conduct experiments on CIFAR-10 with various noise settings and show the results in the table below. First, the results show that LogitClip consistently improves the performance of CE across different depths of ResNet. Second, the performances of both CE and LogitClip are slightly improved with the increase of depth.

| Arch | Method | Sym-20% | Sym-50% | Asymmetric | Dependent | Real |
| -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| ResNet-18     | CE     | 74.94     | 52.25     | 74.39     | 56.53      | 63.16     |
| ResNet-18     | LogitClip     | **84.54**     | **74.24**    | **79.56**     | **76.23**     | **74.65**     |
| ResNet-34     | CE     | 74.16     | 54.48     | 73.94     | 58.03     | 63.24     |
| ResNet-34     | LogitClip     | **84.88**     | **74.81**     | **79.69**     | **76.10**     |  **75.25**     |
| ResNet-50     | CE     | 77.61     | 58.98     | 75.72     | 60.24     | 64.34     |
| ResNet-50     | LogitClip     | **85.53**     | **76.52**     | **80.71**     | **78.83**     | **76.51**     |


5. **How does the method compare to Logit normalization (as in the case of Contrastive Loss calculation)**

We conduct experiments on CIFAR10 with various noisy settings to compare the performance of LogitClip and LogitNorm for learning with noisy labels. The results are presented in the table below. From the comparison, we find that LogitClip is superior to the LogitNorm in this task, especially in those complicated settings. For example, in the asymmetric setting, LogitClip outperforms the LogitNorm method by a large margin (5.1%). Intuitively, LogitNorm can improve the robustness to label noise because it also induces a loss bound. However, it enforces a more strict constraint on all training examples, which may make LogitNorm to be suboptimal in this task. Besides, we give a detailed discussion about our work and LogitNorm [1] in the response to Reviewer iAA1. 


| Method | Sym-50% | Asymmetric | Dependent | Real |
| -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| LogitNorm     | 83.97     | 81.81     | 84.56     | 80.10     |
| LogitClip     | 84.37     | **86.91**     | **86.74**     | **82.06**     |

6. **What happens if the dataset is heavily imbalanced, will the approach remain beneficial?**

We conduct experiments on Long-tailed CIFAR-10 with various settings to validate the benefits of LogitClip under class-imbalanced setting. Here, we fix the imbalance rate as 100. content.summary_of_the_paper: To increase the robustness of CE loss to noisy labels, this paper proposes a method to clamp the model's output. The authors provide detailed theoretical proof that the CE loss is bounded in this LogitClip approach. Also, the authors verify the effectiveness and generality of the method through extensive experiments. The authors' proposed method significantly improves the performance in different kinds of different models and various real scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

This paper is well done from motivation to theoretical analysis as well as experimental validation. We can find evidence from all aspects to support the authors' main claim: the problem of not being able to generate an effective loss for noisy labels due to the unboundedness of CE loss can be largely eliminated by the LogitClip method proposed by the authors. Although it is an extremely simple method, the authors have verified the generality as well as the scalability through a large number of experiments, so we can see the potential capability of this method. Some minor doubts I will raise some in the weakness section.


Weaknesses:
The authors' experiments support the core arguments well. I have a few small additional ablations that I hope the authors can use as references.
1. Although high noise ratios are very rare in real-world scenarios, and the authors' experiments focus on noise ratios around 50%, I am more curious whether the authors' method can still improve performance at high noise ratios.

2. Also, at a 50% noise ratio, I would like to know what is the percentage of logits that are clipped during the training process. Also, is there a direct relationship between the index of the clipped logits and the clean or noisy labels? If the authors can provide some analysis, it will help me to understand the method better.

3. If we do not clip the logits, simply apply an l2 norm to scale the logits, will the performance degrade very much?

4. whether the method logitclip can be used in clean labeled scenarios, such as normal training on a clean dataset like Cifar 100.

content.comment:
Thank you for the valuable comments. Please find our response below.


1. **Can the LogitCLipping method improve performance at high noise ratios?**

Yes, LogitClip can improve the robustness against severely noisy labels. We conduct experiments on CIFAR10 with Symmetric-60% and symmetric-80% noisy labels, and show the test accuracies in the table below. We can observe that the proposed method consistently improves the test performance.

| Method | CIFAR10-Sym-60% | CIFAR10-Sym-80% |  CIFAR100-Sym-60% | CIFAR100-Sym-80% |
| -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| CE     | 60.02     | 39.73     | 38.90     | 19.85     |
| LogitClip     | **77.99**     | **46.47**     | **56.26**     | **25.39**     |



2. **What is the percentage of logits that are clipped during the training process? Is there any relationship between the clipped samples and the noisy samples?**

Thanks for raising interesting questions here. We conduct experiments on CIFAR10 with symmetric-50% noisy labels, and report the clipping rate (CR), and the noise rate of the clipped samples (CNR) in the table below. From the results, we observe that:
* The clipping rate is gradually increasing during the training, from 38.38% to 94.56%. This phenomenon is intuitive as training with cross-entropy loss has been shown to promote a large logit norm.
* The clipped examples are not related to the noisy labels because the noisy rate of the clipped examples is almost equal to that of the whole dataset. 

We hope the analysis provides more insights for in-depth understanding.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper suggests LogitClip, which clips the logit value based on the norm of the logit vector under noise-label training situation. They note that cross entropy loss is not robust to noisy labels due to its unboundedness, while previous robust loss functions achieve robustness on top of that but suffer from underfitting issue. In this regard, they induce loss bounds at logit level while preserving the direction of the original logit vector. They provide theoretical analysis under instance-independent noises which are not real-world scenarios followed by empirical experiments that compared LogitClip with robust loss functions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
1. Adaptivity to existing robust loss functions: Because it handles logit vector's norm, it can easily be incorporated by many existing loss functions.

Weaknesses:
1. Theoretical analysis under unrealistic scenarios: The theoretical analysis is based on the noise-independent scenario, which is easy and ideal case so that it's not compatible with real-world noisy label scenarios. I will wait for the authors' response regarding this weakness.
2. Exhaustive hyperparameter tuning: There is no specific tau value which suceeds across various noise types or datasets. This leads to exhaustive hyperparameter tuning, which is difficult in real-world noisy data training scenarios because acquiring clean ground-truth labels are expensive or even infeasible sometimes. Besides, I'm curious about the result of Webvision data.
3. Outdated related work: There is no related work in 2022; the only reference I can find out is [1] which is for experimental settings. Research on training with noisy labels is extensively studies, so it's inevitable to cover state-of-the-art research outcomes. 

[1] ICLR 2022, A study using real-world human annotations


Questions: 
1. Can you explain the relationship with LogitClip and regularization & reweighting methods?
2. If we clip the logit value, we also hinder a model from learning clean-labeled but hard samples. This, in turn, may lead to the underfitting issue.

content.title: Response to Reviewer mAac
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable comments. Please find our response below.

1. **The theoretical analysis is incompatible with real-world noisy label scenarios.**

Our analysis follows the theoretical framework of previous robust loss functions, such as MAE [1], PHuber-CE [2], SCE [3], GCE [4], Taylor-CE [5], NCE [6], AEL and AUL [7]. It's generally acknowledged that real-world label noise is less tractable from an analytical point of view. Hence, existing works generally conducted theoretical analyses based on instance-independent settings (including symmetric and asymmetric label noises), which are classic and representative. In this work, our analysis adopts exactly the two classic settings and shows how LogitClip strengthens existing functions to be noise-robust. Our analysis gives an in-depth understanding of the connection between logit clipping and label-noise robustness, which we believe is valuable for the research field.

As appreciated by Reviewer 8C9K, we further empirically show that the proposed approach can consistently improve robustness to various settings of label noise, including symmetric, asymmetric, instance-dependent, and real-world settings. While we do not provide theoretical results for all the settings in the paper, the empirical results have extended the generality of the proposed method to those real-world settings.

Lastly, it is worth noting that our analysis can be easily extended to other settings of label noise. _In the revised version, we add an analysis with an instance-dependent setting in Appendix E_. We show that the difference in the risks caused by the derived hypotheses $\tilde{f}$ and $f^{\star}$ under noisy and clean labels is bounded, in this instance-dependent setting.


2. **The hyperparameter tuning might be exhaustive because acquiring clean ground-truth labels are expensive.**

Thank you for pointing this out. To clarify, **the hyperparameter tuning does not require clean validation datasets with ground-truth labels**. Following common practice in the literature of learning from noisy labels [4, 8, 9, 10, 11], we tune the only hyperparameter $\tau$ with a noisy validation set (described in the training details of Subsection 4.1). 

In addition, our theoretical analysis in Proposition 3.1 also provides a principled approach for tuning the $\tau$. As shown in the proposition, the lower bound of the loss value is dependent on the hyperparameter $\tau$ and the class num K. Consequently, we can calculate a rough range of the hyperparameter $\tau$ to achieve a small lower bound. For example, on the CIFAR-10 dataset, the $\tau$ should be larger than 0.83 if we require the training loss to be smaller than 1.0. Based on such an estimation, we can then adjust the value of $\tau$ to find a "sweet spot". Therefore, the parameter can be tuned principally rather than exhaustively.

We also note that most state-of-the-art (SOTA) robust loss functions generally require at least two hyperparameters, whereas LogitNorm only requires one. For example, the hyperparameter numbers of SCE [3], NCE(APL)[6], and AUL[7] are 3, 2, and 2, respectively. As shown in the experimental section, using LogitClip alone (with only one hyperparameter) can achieve superior or comparable performance to these SOTA methods. For example, on the Webvision dataset, using the proposed method alone outperforms the combination of NCE and AGCE, which requires 4 hyperparameters. Therefore, our method is far more efficient than existing SOTA methods from the lens of hyperparameters.



3. **The result of Webvision data.**

We presented the experimental results of the Webvision dataset in **Table 4** and described the results in **Section 4.3**. Following NCE [6], we evaluate the trained networks on the same 50 classes of the ILSVRC12 validation set. In summary, the results show that LogitClip not only outperforms but also enhances existing loss functions by a meaningful margin.


4. **Related works in 2022.**

Thank you for the suggestion. In the revision, we added more recent works in the section of related literature, such as [12, 13, 14]. To the best of our knowledge, we have included almost all recently published works in the area of robust loss functions, that are most relevant to our work. Please feel free to point out specific works that we should be citing, in case we missed any.

(Continue with the next post)

content.title: Response to Reviewer mAac
content.comment:
5. **Relationship between LogitClip and regularization & reweighting methods.**

As shown in the related literature, LogitClip is mostly related to the track of robust loss functions in learning with noisy labels, which is generally a more straightforward and arguably more generic solution with theoretical guarantees. The detailed relationships are described below:

* Regularization: For learning with noisy labels, regularization methods are generally designed to reduce the overfitting to label noise. For example, ODNL [11] introduces OOD examples to consume the extra capacity of the network, thereby reducing the memorization of inherent noisy labels. [10] proposes to use robust early stopping to reduce the side effect of noisy labels before early stopping. In appendix G.2, we also discuss a norm regularization that is derived from our training objective. However, we show such a regularization method can not achieve comparable performance as our method. Those regularization methods are usually conducted with extra data, a new training scheme, or additional training objectives (regularization term). Differently, LogitClip and other robust loss functions directly change the training objective, which generally possesses a theoretical guarantee.

* Reweighting: Reweighting methods aim to design sample weighting schemes that give higher weights on clean samples. For example, MW-Net [15] proposes to adaptively learn an explicit weighting function directly from data. Some loss functions like Focal loss can be also treated as reweighting in the level of loss value. The difference is that robust loss functions are usually designed to implicitly upper bound the negative effect of noisy examples, while reweighting methods explicitly assigned more weight to the clean samples. 


6. **The LogitClip method may cause the underfitting issue on clean data.**

Thank you for raising an interesting point here. We provide both theoretical and empirical evidence to your question:

- Theoretically, as discussed in Section 3 (Proposition 3.1), LogitClip becomes equivalent to vanilla cross-entropy loss if the $\tau$ is large enough. Contrastively, a small $\tau$ will induce a large lower bound on the loss value, which may lead to the underfitting issue.
 - Guided by our theory, we show empirically that LogitClip can indeed achieve comparable performance on the clean CIFAR-100 dataset, with a proper $\tau$.

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their time, insightful suggestions, and valuable comments. We are glad that most reviewers appreciate that our work is well supported by comprehensive experiments on different losses, noise types, architectures, and other potential alternatives (9jkk, 8C9K, iAA1). We are also encouraged that reviewers find this work is novel (8C9K), theoretical supported (9jkk, 8C9K), and shed light on robust loss function direction (mAac). Besides, all the reviewers recognize that this paper is well-organized, clear, and concise.

We respond to each reviewer's comments in detail, respectively. We have also revised the manuscript according to reviewers' suggestions, and we believe this makes our paper much stronger. The main changes we made include:

* In Appendix E, we add an theoretical analysis for an instance-dependent setting as suggested by Reviewer mAac.
* In Appendix G.3, we add an empirical study on a clean dataset to analyze the effect of $\tau$.
* In Appendix E, we add a detail discussion to compare our method to LogitNorm.
* In Section 2, we add some citations to recent published work in learning with noisy labels.
